 Dry weather settles over the Western Slope, with snow possible next week
 Colorado’s November snowpack, despite being weaker in the northern mountains, is far surpassing last year’s numbers
 News News | Nov 9, 2026 
 Andrea Teres-Martinez Follow 
 ateres-martinez@postindependent.com

 The second week of November will be a dry one for Colorado, where snowpack levels are looking considerably better than they did this time last year.
 The break from fall precipitation — bringing a combination of sunny skies and warm temperatures across the Western Slope — is expected to last through at least Friday, Nov. 13, with a chance of moisture possibly arriving in time for the weekend.
 Most mountain towns are forecast to see highs around the mid-50s for the week of Nov. 9, with Thursday and Friday warming up to around 60 degrees. Glenwood Springs and other lower-elevation valleys are expected to stick with highs in the low- to mid-60s throughout the week, according to forecasts from the National Weather Service .
 Snow is expected to return to the forecast the following week, with a low chance of precipitation beginning Saturday, Nov. 14, and a higher chance around Nov. 18-21. But the chances of Saturday’s storm treading high-enough north to bring flakes to the northern mountains are low, according to a Monday OpenSnow report .
 “Through November, you can have wet periods, and you can have dry periods, so I wouldn’t say this is out of the ordinary,” said Kris Sanders, a Grand Junction meteorologist with the National Weather Service. “We are expecting precipitation chances to increase starting this weekend and going into next week. If we do get that precipitation, it would put us above normal at least for the month.”

 Some northern and central-mountain towns — including Vail, Breckenridge, Aspen and Steamboat Springs — could see a chance of rain and snow showers on Saturday night, according to forecasts from the National Weather Service. The weekend precipitation likely won’t last long, however, with most areas expected to return to sunny skies on Sunday, Nov. 15.
 Despite the dry period, new 8-14-day outlooks from the Climate Prediction Center show Colorado has a roughly 60% chance of receiving above-average precipitation through the middle of the month, paired with what will likely be slightly above-average temperatures.
 Colorado snowpack cruises past 2025 figures 
 According to data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, Colorado’s snowpack is right around average for this time of year, a welcome start following last year’s record-low snowfall . Sanders said the snowpack in western Colorado is sitting at 99% of normal for Nov. 9, with roughly five months until what is historically considered Colorado’s peak snowpack.
 During this time last year, the snowpack was at 25% of normal for the western region, meaning Colorado is significantly ahead where it was in 2025.
 Not everywhere has had the same luck, however. While southern Colorado’s snowpack is well above-average for the second week of November, some sub-basins in the northern mountains are closer to 25% of median snow water equivalent, as recent storms have targeted the southwestern corner of the state.
 “A lot of the basins north of I-70 are actually fairly low,” Sanders said. “When you get down to the San Juan (mountains), you’re looking at like 200% to 300% of normal, so the southern half of the state has definitely been keeping up those numbers.”
 Four Colorado ski resorts have opened for the 2026-27 season as of Nov. 9, all located in the northern mountains: Arapahoe Basin, Keystone, Loveland Ski Area and Copper Mountain. Wolf Creek Ski Area in southwest Colorado celebrated its opening day on Halloween but had to close shortly after opening due to severe regional flooding.
 Other resorts scattered across the northern and central mountains are scheduled to open throughout the remainder of November, including Breckenridge Ski Resort (Nov. 11), Steamboat Ski Resort (Nov. 21), Aspen Mountain (Nov. 26) and Snowmass (Nov. 26).
